findings.name: billing
findings.root_cause: The billing container uses envFrom to load ConfigMap "billing-config", which does not exist in the billing namespace (only kube-root-ca.crt is present), so kubelet fails with CreateContainerConfigError and the pod stays Pending.
findings.fix: Create the missing ConfigMap billing-config in namespace billing with the keys the app expects (or remove/point the envFrom reference at an existing ConfigMap).

diagnosis.summary: billing Deployment's pod is stuck Pending with CreateContainerConfigError: its container references ConfigMap \"billing-config\" via envFrom, but that ConfigMap does not exist in the billing namespace. Creating the ConfigMap (or fixing the reference) will let the pod start.

findings.name: orders-api
findings.root_cause: orders-api container starts, fails to load config because DATABASE_URL is not set (no env or envFrom in the pod spec), exits 1 and crash-loops; with 0/1 ready replicas the orders page has no backend.
findings.fix: Add DATABASE_URL to the orders-api Deployment (env from a Secret/ConfigMap or an existing DB service) so the container can start; then restart the rollout.

diagnosis.summary: orders/orders-api crashes on startup: logs show 'FATAL: DATABASE_URL is not set' and exit code 1, with 5 restarts and BackOff events. The pod spec has no env/envFrom at all, so the deployment never provides DATABASE_URL. No ConfigMap/Secret exists in the namespace that could supply it. Fix: add the missing database URL configuration to the orders-api Deployment.

findings.name: mailer
findings.root_cause: mailer crash-loops with 'nc: bad address smtp-relay' because its pod template sets dnsPolicy None with a bogus nameserver 10.96.0.99, so in-cluster DNS resolution of the smtp-relay service fails; the relay itself is healthy (pod Running, Service has 1 ready endpoint).
findings.fix: Remove the custom dnsConfig/dnsPolicy None from the mailer Deployment pod template (or set dnsPolicy ClusterFirst) so pods use the cluster DNS at 10.96.0.10.

diagnosis.summary: The relay is not down: smtp-relay pod is Running and its Service has 1 ready endpoint on port 25. The mailer crash-loop is a DNS misconfiguration — the mailer Deployment's pod template overrides DNS with dnsPolicy None and nameserver 10.96.0.99, so resolving 'smtp-relay' fails ('nc: bad address') and the container exits after 3 attempts, triggering BackOff restarts. Fix: drop the custom dnsConfig (use default ClusterFirst) in the mailer Deployment."

findings.name: stock-db
findings.root_cause: stock-db's 24Mi memory limit is exceeded during its 'loading stock index' phase, so the container is OOMKilled (exit 137) in a restart loop and never becomes ready. The stock-db Service then has no ready endpoints, stock-api cannot reach stock-db:5432, exhausts 3 retries and crash-loops.
findings.fix: Raise the stock-db Deployment's memory request/limit well above 24Mi (e.g. 256Mi or more, sized to the stock-index load) so the container survives the index load and stays up; stock-api will then connect and stop restarting.

diagnosis.summary: Root cause: stock-db runs with a 24Mi memory limit; its 'loading stock index into memory' phase exceeds it, so kubelet OOMKills it (exit 137, repeated BackOff). The pod is 0/1 ready and the stock-db Service has zero ready endpoints. Consequence: stock-api logs 'stock-db:5432 unreachable', exits after 3 attempts ('FATAL: database unavailable') and crash-loops — it is a victim of the DB being down. Fix: raise stock-db's memory limit to cover the index load; no LimitRange or quota involved.

findings.name: defaults
findings.root_cause: statement-builder's Deployment sets no memory resources, so the namespace LimitRange 'defaults' injects a 32Mi memory limit; the workload needs more than 32Mi to build statements, so the kernel OOM-kills it (exit 137) and it crash-loops.
findings.fix: Set an explicit memory limit/request on the statement-builder container (e.g. 256Mi) large enough for its peak usage, or raise/remove the 32Mi default in LimitRange 'defaults'.

diagnosis.summary: statement-builder in finance is OOMKilled (exit 137, 3 restarts) even though its Deployment defines no memory limits. Root cause: the namespace LimitRange 'defaults' applies a 32Mi default memory limit (16Mi request) to containers without explicit resources, and the statement-building workload exceeds 32Mi. Fix by giving the container an explicit, adequate memory limit or adjusting the LimitRange.

findings.name: checkout
findings.root_cause: Calls to the checkout service fail with connection refused because the Service selector app=checkout-v2 matches no pods (the Deployment labels its pods app=checkout), so it has 0 ready endpoints and traffic is dropped/refused even though the pod itself is healthy.
findings.fix: Align the selector: change the Service selector to app=checkout (or relabel the Deployment's pod template to app=checkout-v2) so it matches the running pods, then verify ready endpoints appear.

diagnosis.summary: The checkout pod is healthy (1/1 ready, no problem pods, only normal events). The failure is in the Service: checkout/checkout selects app=checkout-v2 while the Deployment's pods are labeled app=checkout, so the Service has 0 matching pods and 0 ready endpoints — clients get connection refused. Fix the selector mismatch on either the Service or the Deployment pod template.

findings.name: report-worker
findings.root_cause: The report-worker container is OOMKilled (exit 137) every few seconds because its memory limit is only 32Mi, so it restarts in a crash loop with no application error in the logs.
findings.fix: Raise the report-worker container's memory limit (e.g. to 128Mi or more, matching observed usage) and adjust the request accordingly; then redeploy.

diagnosis.summary: report-worker in namespace reports crash-loops: the pod is repeatedly OOMKilled (exit code 137) because the Deployment sets a 32Mi memory limit on the busybox container running `tail /dev/zero`. findings.fix: Point the readiness probe at the port nginx actually serves (httpGet port 80), or make the container listen on 8081 (e.g. set the containerPort / nginx listen directive).

diagnosis.summary: web/web-7969d6cc4c-46fdj runs nginx:1.29-alpine with no custom config, so it serves on port 80, while the Deployment's readiness probe targets port 8081. The probe fails with 'connection refused' (25 warnings), the pod is NotReady, and the Deployment has 0 ready replicas — matching the report of 0/1 ready with a running container. No Service exists in the namespace, so nothing else consumes endpoints; the root cause is the probe/port mismatch in the web Deployment spec.

findings.name: team-quota
findings.root_cause: renderer was scaled to 5 replicas, but the batch namespace ResourceQuota team-quota limits pods to 2 (already used: 2), so ReplicaSet renderer-85d9d4b59d cannot create the remaining 3 pods — every FailedCreate reports 'exceeded quota: team-quota, requested: pods=1, used: pods=2, limited: pods=2'.
findings.fix: Raise the pods limit in ResourceQuota team-quota in namespace batch from 2 to at least 5 (or move renderer to a namespace/quota with enough pod capacity), then let the ReplicaSet create the missing pods.

diagnosis.summary: renderer Deployment in batch is stuck at 2 of 5 ready replicas because ResourceQuota team-quota caps pods at 2 (used: 2). Events show repeated FailedCreate on ReplicaSet renderer-85d9d4b59d with 'exceeded quota: team-quota ... limited: pods=2', and the Deployment has a ReplicaFailure condition citing the same quota. No pod-level faults; the root cause is the quota object itself. Fix: raise the pods hard limit in team-quota to >= 5."
